paper_title: Mine, Sample, Render: Test-Time Diversity Alignment Of Generative Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE-SAMPLE-RENDER (MSR), a test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from a corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses a generative model purely as a conditional renderer of a sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: Modern generative models produce high-quality individual outputs but struggle to sample diversely, even when explicitly instructed to do so. We introduce MINE SAMPLERENDER (MSR), test-time approach that externalizes the diversity into an explicit, corpus-derived sampling procedure. Our pipeline (i) mines an interpretable categorical schema from corpus of real artifacts and supplies statistics for sampling; (ii) samples attribute configurations from the corpus-derived statistics; (iii) uses generative model purely as conditional renderer of sampled configuration. Across weather report generation, user simulation, webpage design, text-to-image generation, and agent-generated 3D assets, we evaluate the diversity and output quality of MSR-guided generation and show that MSR improves alignment with corpus distributions and diversity of generated outputs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Many applications of generative AI require diverse samples, not just individually plausible outputs. Synthetic datasets (Huang et al., 2025) and simulated user populations should reflect the variation in the populations they represent. Diverse exploration can also improve reasoning and generalization in LLMs (Liu et al., 2025), while in text-to-image models, diversity in generations directly drives their test-time scaling capability (Rawal et al., 2026). Yet modern generators (and even tool-using agents) often sample much narrower range of variation than what is typically found in real data. This gap has been observed in user simulation (Mehri et al., 2026), engineering design (Ma et al., 2025), creative ideation (Anderson et al., 2024), and story generation (Xu et al., 2025b), and is exacerbated by reward-maximizing post-training (e.g., Shao et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2023) which is commonly used to improve model quality, but can further concentrate samples around high-reward modes and suppress less common but valid alternatives (Hu et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026). Changing the prompt does change the output, creating an impression of variety, but every prompt leaves choices unspecified, and models repeatedly resolve them in the same way (Figure 1). Simply increasing temperature or asking model to be diverse does not identify what should vary, how often, or which combinations are plausible. Even visibly different generations may cover little of the variation in real data, and convincing outputs can therefore be collectively homogeneous; even when each user asks for only one. Just give me one good webpage does not mean make it look like everyone elses. single coherent, correct output can still feel obviously AI-generated. We pursue test-time diversity alignment: bringing the distribution of generated outputs into closer agreement with the real-data distribution relevant to the task. reference corpus supplies an empirical targetwhat varies, how often, and in which combinations. The relevant examples or regularities may already have appeared during pretraining, but that variation is not reliably recovered in the deployed models samples. Crucially, off-the-shelf models can often identify meaningful differences among real examples and produce the corresponding attributes when explicitly instructed. We introduce MINESAMPLERENDER (MSR), shown in Figure 2. In one-time preprocessing stage for given reference corpus, MSR compares small cohorts of artifacts to discover attributes, then labels the corpus to estimate their joint distribution. To generate new artifact, it samples an attribute configuration from this distribution and asks generative model or tool-using agent to render it. This separates what can be generated from how often it should be generated. Work done during research internship at Microsoft.

MSR relates to attribute-guided generation (Yu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025), persona conditioning (Moon et al., 2024; Ge et al., 2024), and quality-diversity search (Bradley et al., 2024). Its mining step connects to work on data-induced semantic features and concepts (Jojic & Jojic, 2025; Zhong et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2024; Pham et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2024), while separating structure from realization has precedents in hierarchical text and layout generation (Fan et al., 2018; Inoue et al., 2023). close generative precursor is fLSA (Xu et al., 2025a), which learns natural-language segment tags through reconstruction-based fitting, and samples tag sequences before rendering text. MSRs distinguishing contribution is to discover compositional, artifact-level attributes through direct cohort comparisons and sample their corpus-estimated joint distribution to guide generation. An expanded discussion of related research appears in Appendix A. We apply MSR to multiple diverse domains: (i) in controlled setting of synthetically generated weather reports with known axes of variation, we show that the mining stage can recover the real axes of variation that were used in generating the dataset and that the sampling can reproduce their joint distribution faithfully, (ii) in synthetic user simulation, we show that MSR reduces the distributional gap between LLM-simulated and real user behavior, (iii) in open-ended webpage design with LLMs, MSR greatly improves the diversity of generated webpages over prompt-only baselines, (iv) in text-to-image generation, MSR improves the sample diversity of state-of-the-art textto-image generative models, and (v) in 3D asset generation with tool-using agents we show that MSR increases both the diversity and quality of generated assets.

The LLM is given set of artifacts and asked to identify attributes that are either shared by some artifacts or vary within the cohort. This process is performed in parallel for large number of cohorts, resulting in small schemas that were mined independently, possibly containing overlapping or synonymous attributes. We consolidate these into single schema by using an LLM to merge synonymous attributes. We then back-apply the consolidated schema to the source corpus, producing sparse occurrence matrix from which we estimate attribute frequencies and dependencies. 2.2 SAMPLING SPARSE CONFIGURATIONS We use the occurrence matrix to estimate joint distribution over attributes and sample configurations with ϕ. We explore two approaches: topic-based sampling and sequential ancestral sampling, which conditions each draw on preceding assignments. Conditioning on request. Users supply ordinary-language requests without needing to know the attribute vocabulary. For small schema, an LLM could identify required and compatible attributes directly from their descriptions; we do not evaluate that alternative here. For large schemas, we augment the statistical representation with lexical features: TFIDF-selected words and shared n-grams from attribute names and descriptions. Each source artifact inherits features from its present attributes, supplemented by caption terms when available. These shared features provide conditioning evidence when the request does not match complete attribute description. Both mined attributes and lexical features can condition sampling. Explicit requirements, such as left-hand navigation in webpage, may be fixed; compatibility identifies eligible candidates, while lexical matches supply statistical evidence. sections.title: 3.2 USER SIMULATION
sections.content: We apply MINESAMPLERENDER to the task of using LLMs to simulate users that interact with LLM assistants. Given high-level user goal, an LLM generates plausible user trajectory, while another LLM provides assistant responses. In the mining stage, we compare real user-LLM interactions and mine attributes that describe user behavior. Then we sample an attribute configuration and use it to condition user simulator, which interacts with an assistant. We evaluate the gap between held-out distribution of real users and simulated distribution of users with the same user goal using the evaluation protocol introduced by Mehri et al. (2026). Implementation. We focus on simulating users for coding tasks and use the same dataset of 5000 real coding conversations used by Mehri et al. (2026) for evaluation. We mine distinct set of 600 real coding conversations from WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024) to use for schema generation. We use 2 different mining prompts to recover attributes at different granularities, resulting in 2 schemas with 84 (compact) and 465 (fine-grained) attributes, respectively. For our experiments, we use GPT-5mini as the miner. We fix GPT-5.4 as the assistant and compare four user-simulation conditions: prompt only, using coding-relevant PersonaHub persona (Ge et al., 2024), and sampled attribute configurations with both schemas. We specifically filter for personas suited to coding tasks and sample from this subset uniformly with replacement when simulating users. sections.title: 3.3 WEBPAGE GENERATION
sections.content: Prior work reports convergence in the visual appearance of user interfaces produced by LLM-based generation tools (Imteyaz et al., 2026), while practitioner accounts describe recurring aesthetic and design defaults in LLM-generated webpages (Anthropic, 2025). We make the same observation: LLM-generated webpages tend to collapse to very specific look and design structure (Figure 4). In this setting, we apply MINESAMPLERENDER to improve the diversity of generated pages given some fixed provided content. In the mining stage, VLM is given the HTML code and screenshot for cohort of webpages and asked to compare them to produce schema of design attributes. For sampling, we sample attributes with ancestral sampling (Section 2.2.2) while also identifying and including attributes specified by the initial prompt using an LLM. Implementation. We use two different datasets to mine schema to assess how data complexity and scale affect its quality and usefulness. We mine the first schema of 485 attributes using GPT-5mini from 10,000 webpages sourced from WebSight v0.1 (Laurencon et al., 2024), which contains simple, synthetically generated webpages. For the second schema, we use the 484 more realistic and complex webpages in the Design2Code dataset (Si et al., 2025) and mine 5,484 attributes using GPT5.6 Sol. For evaluation, we use 100 webpage authoring prompts paired with grounding documents that contain the desired content (images, text), and GPT-5.5 or Kimi K2.6 as the generator. As baseline, we prompt an LLM generator with just the website authoring prompt and the grounding documents. For each prompt, we generate 10 webpages with each method and measure the diversity of the generated sets of webpages using the Vendi Score (Friedman & Dieng, 2023) in two different settings: (i) we render screenshots of the generated webpages, embed them using DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024), and calculate the Vendi Score based on the similarity of the image embeddings; (ii) we strip the HTML pages of their content, keeping only the structural elements as text, embed them using OpenAIs text-embedding-3-large model, and calculate the Vendi Score based on the similarity of the text embeddings. Implementation. We use up to 100 images from each category of the training set of MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014) and mine schema of 28,875 properties using GPT-5.6 Sol. We fit 20-topic model on compact, support-filtered vocabulary of 350 mined attributes and 450 lexical features. The topic component captures shared modes of variation rather than attempting to preserve the full range of rare attributes and their specific dependencies. The ancestral component retains access to the full schema through request-specific pool of at most 250 attributes, allowing more specific details to be sampled when supported by the corpus. We sample with mix between topic and ancestral sampling with λ = 0.5. Topic draws introduce broad variation, while ancestral draws condition on previously selected attributesincluding those drawn from topicsto introduce empirically compatible details. Feature-selection criteria and sampling details are provided in Appendix B.5. We evaluate GPT Image 2, MAI-Image-2.5, and FLUX.2-flex on 50 held-out MS-COCO validation captions, one from each of 50 categories, with ten images per caption and arm. We compare five arms: prompt only, independent rewrite, coordinated rewrite, MSRDirect, and MSRResolved. Prompt rewriting is widely used in text-to-image generation (Betker et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2025) and evaluation (Kamath et al., 2025). Our independent baseline rewrites the original request in separate LLM calls; the coordinated baseline produces set of rewrites in one call aiming to improve their diversity. MSRDirect provides the sampled attributes to the generators directly, while MSRResolved passes them to an LLM that first resolves placeholders and composes coherent scene instructions. Both variants may omit attributes that cannot be realized plausibly alongside the request and other retained attributes. GPT-5.6 Sol performs both baseline rewriting

Here we ask more demanding question: when capable model can plan, write code, use tools, and iterate and revise generated outputs, does it nevertheless repeatedly choose narrow range of designs? sections.title: 4 CONCLUSION
sections.content: While modern generative models excel at producing high-quality individual outputs, they inherently struggle to generate diverse outputs and reproduce the distribution of real populations. To address this limitation, we introduced MINESAMPLERENDER (MSR), training-free framework that decouples the statistical sampling of implicit generative choices from the generation step itself. By mining interpretable categorical schemas from real-world corpora and explicitly sampling attribute configurations, MSR allows the underlying model to act purely as conditional renderer.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Our evaluations across highly varied domainsspanning weather reports, user simulations, web design, image generation, and agent-created 3D assetsdemonstrate that MSR significantly enhances output diversity and aligns generated populations with real distributions. Ultimately, MSR provides robust, interpretable mechanism for ensuring generative models can capture the full richness and variability of real-world data.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools to draft sections of the paper, to find related work, and to aid or polish writing. Specifically, we created initial drafts of implementation detail sections by providing an LLM with the source code and requesting text report. Authors verified the provided text and edited it for clarity. Additionally, we used LLMs to find and gather related literature, which the authors reviewed, and to rewrite parts of the paper to improve clarity. We also used generative AI tools for generating synthetic data sets and implementing methods. We implemented our method using coding agents and reviewed and verified the generated code for correctness. The dataset of 100 prompts and grounding documents used for evaluating webpage generation was generated with an LLM and filtered by the authors. sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: From explicit attributes to data-induced semantic variables. common temptation when using foundation models is to ask them to perform both semantic and statistical reasoning in one unconstrained call: invent the latent variables, decide which ones matter, determine how they are distributed, and generate an artifact. AttrPrompt and DataGen instead condition generation on explicit attributes obtained through user specification, LLM prior knowledge, or selected in-context examples (Yu et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025), but do not estimate the source populations joint distribution: diversity comes from random attribute combinations, LLM prompting, or post-hoc filtering. Persona Hub conditions generation on sampled persona records, while QDAIF iteratively searches user-specified behavior space for high-quality distinct outputs (Ge et al., 2024; Bradley et al., 2024); these approaches likewise externalize diversity without estimating target corpuss joint distribution over compositional attributes. This matters because the semantic diversity potentially encoded during training is not reliably exposed at generation time; repeated LLM outputs reproduce narrow set of plot patterns compared with human corpora and human ideation or design processes (Xu et al., 2025b; Anderson et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). We therefore treat the corpus as external memory: the foundation model rediscovers human-readable dimensions by comparing observed artifacts, while conventional statistics estimates how those dimensions are distributed. This division follows two hybrid statisticalfoundational models that mine semantic features through generalized EM but optimize different likelihoods. GenZ (Jojic & Jojic, 2025) optimizes the conditional likelihood p(y x), linking semantic item to an external, possibly high-dimensional numerical target through latent semantic features. Its statistical model uses target residuals to identify useful split; foundation model names the distinction and applies that natural-language question to all items. Refitting tests the resulting feature, and contraction removes features that do not preserve useful target structure. GenZ therefore produces readable, reusable semantic hypotheses paired with quantitative evidence, but it neither models the population p(x) nor renders new artifacts. fLSA (Xu et al., 2025a), by contrast, targets p(x) through reconstruction-like likelihood. It represents each document segment with one of fixed number of natural-language tags and alternates between assigning segments to tags and rewriting each tag from its assigned segments. After learning, fLSA fits bigram model over tags, samples tag sequence as an outline, and renders text conditioned on that outline. MINESAMPLERENDER differs first in the statistical object it learns. fLSA models sequence of one-of-K segment tags, while GenZ uses multiple binary semantic features to predict y. MINE SAMPLERENDER instead represents each artifact by compositional attribute configuration, fits joint distribution over configurations, and renders from sampled configurations. More importantly, MINESAMPLERENDER learns these semantic coordinates differently. fLSA iteratively refines segment-level tags through assignment and summarization. In contrast, we use direct comparisons among artifacts within small cohorts to propose the semantic coordinates in which the population will be modeled. Our objective is not to recover every semantic mode exhaustively, but to expose meaningful population variation that direct generation systematically underrepresents. The semantic contrasts used here have closer relatives in GenZ and D5. GenZ shows the foundation model two statistically constructed groups whose split is directed by y. D5 compares two predefined corpora and asks for natural-language differences between them (Zhong et al., 2023). In MINE SAMPLERENDER, the cohorts are unpartitioned: the foundation model enumerates all attributes that recur or vary among their members. Near-duplicate proposals are consolidated, and every retained attribute is back-applied to the full corpus. Local comparisons therefore propose the vocabulary, while global labeling determines its empirical frequencies and dependencies. LLooM, TopicGPT, and TnT-LLM similarly induce natural-language concepts or taxonomies and assign them back to corpus, while natural-language-parameterized statistical models optimize such predicates for clustering, classification, or time-series objectives (Lam et al., 2024; Pham et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024); these methods analyze observed data rather than sampling joint configuration distribution for rendering. Sampling sparse attribute configurations. Once artifacts are labeled, sampling becomes classical discrete density-estimation problem. Resampling observed configurations preserves the em-

sections.content: pirical joint but cannot form new combinations; independent marginals do so while discarding all dependencies. ChowLiu trees provide tractable middle ground by retaining the strongest pairwise mutual-information dependencies (Chow & Liu, 1968), while count backoff in language models retains specific contexts only when they have adequate support (Katz, 1987). Our sampler is pragmatic higher-order variant: under fresh random variable ordering, it ranks previously sampled attributes by mutual information with the next attribute, retains the largest sufficiently supported conditioning set, smooths the resulting conditional, and masks incompatible values. We do not claim ancestral sampling, mutual information, or backoff as new; the contribution is their combination for sparse, corpus-induced semantic configurations. Structured conditional generation. Hierarchical text generation separates plans or outlines from prose (Fan et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2025a), while scene-layout models separate explicit object and spatial structure from pixel rendering. LayoutVAE and LayoutDM additionally learn distributions over structured layouts before rendering (Jyothi et al., 2019; Inoue et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2023). Work such as Design2Code demonstrates increasingly capable screenshotconditioned webpage rendering (Si et al., 2025), but optimizes the fidelity of one page rather than diversity among pages generated for the same request. These works validate separating structure from realization; MINESAMPLERENDER instead induces the semantic control space itself from corpus and samples from corpus-estimated distribution over attribute configurations before invoking replaceable conditional renderer. Population-level evaluation. Recent work finds that individually plausible LLM user simulators remain distributionally different from real users and are often overly cooperative or behaviorally uniform (Mehri et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026). When target population is observed, divergence and coverage measure whether generated frequencies match it; for open-ended sets without unique target distribution, the Vendi Score provides reference-free effective-diversity measure, while qualityfiltered semantic diversity excludes varied but invalid outputs (Friedman & Dieng, 2023; Shypula et al., 2025). These distinctions motivate evaluating distributional fidelity, set diversity, condition adherence, and per-output acceptability separately.

sections.title: B IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS
sections.content: B.1 ANCESTRAL SAMPLING With conditioning on the user request implicit, we draw random attribute ordering π and sample each attribute aπj sequentially using its conditional probability given preceding assignments, p(aπj aπ1, . . . , aπj1 ). However, as increases, exact empirical conditionals suffer from data sparsity; strictly enforcing them would restrict the sampler to reproducing only exact combinations present in the source dataset. To enable generalization beyond the training data, we dynamically reduce the conditioning set: we rank the previously sampled attributes by their mutual information with aπj and retain only the highest-ranked subset such that minimum support threshold of source rows remains. Letting be this final supported set of source rows, we estimate the conditional probability using additive smoothing: (cid:98)q(aπj = S) = nv(S) + β + βKj , where nv(S) counts the rows in with value v, Kj is the total number of possible values, and β is the smoothing parameter. Finally, to ensure logical coherence, we enforce pairwise compatibility mask generated offline by an LLM, which reviews schema descriptions to identify mutually exclusive property pairs. During sampling, any candidate value that conflicts with previously selected attribute is assigned zero probability, and the remaining valid options are renormalized.

sections.content: B.2 WEATHER REPORTS B.2.1 DATASET CONSTRUCTION This controlled experiment uses synthetic text grounded in real weather observations, rather than independently sampled weather attributes. We obtain daily historical weather from the Open-Meteo archive for Phoenix, Reykjavik, Singapore, London, Seattle, Cairo, Moscow, Mumbai, Sydney, and Denver. The training year is 2016, with 366 days per city and 3,660 city-day records. The heldout year is 2017, with 365 days per city and 3,650 records. We apply the same discretization to both years along four categorical weather axes, each with four possible values, represented as 16 binary attributes with one active value per axis. Ten additional one-hot city indicators give 26 binary attributes in the complete source record. City is conditioning variable throughout evaluation, not one of the weather axes whose joint distribution is scored. Temperature. Daily mean temperature is binned as cold below 8C, mild from 8C to below 18C, warm from 18C to below 27C, and hot at or above 27C. Sky. Weather codes 45 and 48 take precedence and map to foggy. Otherwise, mean cloud cover below 25% maps to clear, from 25% to below 60% to partly cloudy, and at least 60% to overcast. Wind. Gusty takes precedence when the daily maximum gust is at least 60 km/h or the maximum 10 wind speed is at least 40 km/h. Otherwise, maximum wind speed at least 25 km/h maps to windy, at least 12 km/h to breezy, and below 12 km/h to calm. Thus, windy and gusty are distinct source categories. Precipitation. Weather codes 95, 96, and 99 map to storm. Otherwise, snowfall greater than 0.1 cm or snow code in {71, 73, 75, 77, 85, 86} maps to snow. Among the remaining days, precipitation at least 1 mm or rain code in {51, 53, 55, 56, 57, 61, 63, 65, 66, 67, 80, 81, 82} maps to rain; all other days map to none. The precedence is storm, then snow, then rain, then none. In preprocessing, days with missing mean temperature are skipped; missing cloud cover defaults to 50%, and missing wind, gust, precipitation, snowfall, or weather-code values are treated as zero. B.2.2 RECOVERED SCHEMA AND ANNOTATION The retained discovery request compares 299 source reports together in single call; one report is held out from vocabulary discovery. The prompt asks what is shared and what differs, then requests binary, atomic properties named by category prefix and realization suffix, with supporting quotation. It does not receive the numerical discretization rules or the predefined property menu. This produces 13 weather attributes across temperature, sky, wind, and precipitation. City is supplied separately rather than discovered as weather attribute. Table 5 shows both successful recovery and its limits. The recovered schema distinguishes all four temperature values and three values each for sky, wind, and precipitation. Foggy and storm have zero support in the source configurations, and neither occurs in the retained full-year tuples for 2016 or 2017. By contrast, windy occurs in 24 source configurations but has no separate recovered value. Its absence cannot be explained by zero source support, although this comparison alone cannot distinguish source-rendering failure from mining failure. Page JavaScript and service workers are disabled, external HTTP(S) requests are blocked, and animations and transitions are suppressed. We wait for fonts and image decoding, force image loading to be eager, and reject pages with fewer than 100 characters of rendered body text or any broken images. These checks establish basic renderability, not content fidelity or usability. For page of height H, we capture viewport screenshots at vertical positions zero, the rounded midpoint of the scroll range, and the bottom of the scroll range, where the maximum scroll is max(0, 768). Each capture follows 100-ms settling interval. Short pages can therefore have identical views. We retain all three screenshots, giving 9,000 screenshots per generator. Odd-one-out evaluation uses only the top view; visual diversity uses all three. B.4.6 ODD-ONE-OUT EVALUATION For each task and generator, we separately compare each schema-conditioned set against the promptonly set. Each comparison begins with pool of ten baseline and ten schema-conditioned top-view screenshots. Screenshots receive neutral numeric labels, and the judge is asked to identify the single page whose visual design is most unlike the others, considering layout, colour, typography, spacing, and components. The judge receives screenshots, not HTML, schema identifiers, or condition labels. We use GPT-5-mini with low reasoning effort and 2,048-token completion budget. Each response must contain valid JSON object identifying an in-pool label and short reason; malformed responses receive up to two additional parsing attempts rather than substituted selection. After each decision, we remove the selected page and reshuffle and relabel the remaining pool. We stop after ten removals and repeat the complete cascade four times. Shuffle seeds are derived deterministically from the experiment seed, task, schema condition, repetition, and round. This yields 200 task-schema comparisons and 8,000 removal decisions per generator. We report the fraction of removals attributable to the schema-conditioned set, with 4,000 removals as the denominator for each schema-generator pair. We also report mean removal rank: the ten removed pages receive ranks one through ten in removal order, while every surviving page receives rank 20, not an inferred rank between 11 and 20. Ranks are averaged across repetitions and pages within condition, then equally across tasks. The baseline rank is comparison-specific because it depends on the competing schema-conditioned pool. Larger removal shares and smaller ranks indicate greater stylistic distinctiveness in these mixed pools; neither is quality-preference or task-success measure. Its limited coverage motivated targeted searches for additional chair families and appearances: camping and directors chairs, deckchairs, transparent seating, shaped or painted timber, leather, cane, perforated panels, bamboo and historical scissor forms. Queries included named design examples such as Plia, Rex and Trieste, and non-English terms such as Klappstuhl, chaise pliante and sedia pieghevole. The final corpus has 160 curated design/appearance records and 305 selected evidence images. It includes 159 folding-chair records and one explicitly identified demountable chair.
